basics.name: Adhesive manufacturers' selection and design guides: Henkel LOCTITE Design Guides (Bonding Plastics Vol. 6, Bonding Metals Vol. 6, Bonding Rubber and TPEs Vol. 3) and the LOCTITE Adhesive Sourcebook; 3M Scotch-Weld Structural Adhesives Product Selection Guide and white paper 'Choosing and Using a Structural Adhesive'; Permabond Adhesive Guide and '5 Steps to choosing the best adhesive'
basics.url: Main example: LOCTITE Design Guide for Bonding Plastics, Vol. 6 (LT-2197, 2011), distributor-hosted PDF https://www.ellsworth.com/globalassets/literature-library/manufacturer/henkel-loctite/henkel-loctite-design-guide-plastic-bonding.pdf (opened). Also opened: Henkel-hosted Metals guide https://dm.henkel-dam.com/is/content/henkel/Metal_Bonding_Guide.pdf; Henkel-hosted Rubber/TPE guide https://dm.henkel-dam.com/is/content/henkel/lt-2662a-brochure-design-guide-for-bonding-rubber-and-thermoplastic-elastomers-volume-3-2011; LOCTITE Adhesive Sourcebook 2017 Vol. 20 https://www.ellsworth.com/globalassets/literature-library/manufacturer/henkel-loctite/henkel-loctite-adhesive-sourcebook-2015.pdf; 3M Product Selection Guide (June 2024) https://multimedia.3m.com/mws/media/328280O/product-selection-guide.pdf; 3M white paper https://multimedia.3m.com/mws/media/795693O/choosing-and-using-a-structural-adhesive-white-paper.pdf; Permabond Adhesive Guide (2023, distributor copy) https://tewipack.de/fileadmin/website/service/downloads/produktinfos/permabond/permabond-adhesive-guide-2023-en.pdf; Permabond article https://permabond.com/adhesive-selection-5-steps-to-choosing-the-best-adhesive-for-your-situation/
basics.resource_type: PDF design guide (manufacturer technical literature: design guides, selector guides and catalogues with comparison tables; 3M also runs an online interactive selector)
basics.cost: Free. The PDFs download without login from manufacturer or distributor sites. Printed copies were historically free on request
basics.license: All rights reserved (e.g. '© Henkel Corporation, 2011. All rights reserved'; 3M and Permabond material is copyrighted and trademarked). Link to them and cite facts (e.g. 'cyanoacrylates rate Poor on glass'), but don't copy the tables, figures or text. Product names are trademarks and are out of scope for the encyclopedia anyway
basics.language: English (the versions opened). Henkel, 3M and Permabond publish regional versions in other languages [uncertain]
basics.year: LOCTITE Plastics guide: a multi-volume series (volumes 1 and 2 compounded and tested the 30 plastics; the date of volume 1 wasn't found [uncertain]), Volume 6 dated 2011 (LT-2197). Rubber/TPE Vol. 3: 2011 (LT-2662A). Metals Vol. 6: © 2014 (LT-3371; PDF file dated 2019). Adhesive Sourcebook: 2017, Vol. 20. 3M Product Selection Guide: June 2024 edition. 3M white paper: 2018. Permabond Adhesive Guide: 2023 (edited 2024). Permabond '5 steps' article: 28 January 2009
basics.access_barrier: none (free PDF download). Some manufacturer sites block automated access or need a region choice, but distributor mirrors (e.g. Ellsworth) are open. 3M's online selector is a web app
basics.image_license: All rights reserved (manufacturer photos, joint-design and stress-distribution diagrams, bar charts)
basics.authority_level: manufacturer (the technical departments of Henkel, 3M and Permabond, based on their own lab testing, e.g. Henkel's block-shear tests on 30 plastics and 26 rubbers/TPEs; commercially biased toward their own products)

coverage.covers: Adhesive chemistries compared by substrate, strength, flexibility, temperature and chemical resistance, gap filling and cure method, plus surface preparation and joint design. Henkel Plastics guide: 7 adhesive families (cyanoacrylate, epoxy, hot melt, light-curing acrylic, polyurethane, silicone, no-mix and static-mix acrylic) tested on 30 plastic families (acetal, acrylic/PMMA, ABS, ASA, nylon, polycarbonate, polyethylene, polypropylene, PTFE and other fluoropolymers, PVC, PET, polystyrene, PEEK, PPS and others), plus a stress-cracking compatibility table, 12 or 13 surface treatments and a joint-design chapter. Henkel Metals guide: 7 families (two-step acrylic, two-part acrylic, cyanoacrylate, epoxy, hot melt, polyurethane, elastomer) on 8 metals and finishes (aluminium, anodised aluminium, copper, nickel, stainless steel, steel, zinc-dichromated steel, galvanised steel). Henkel Rubber/TPE guide: 8 families on 26 rubbers and thermoplastic elastomers (butyl, EPDM, natural rubber, neoprene, nitrile, silicone, SBR, TPV, styrenic TPE and others). LOCTITE Sourcebook: a one-page comparison of 9 adhesive categories (cyanoacrylates, epoxies, hot melts, light cure, silicones, elastomers, urethanes, two-part acrylics, two-step acrylics), each rated Poor/Fair/Good/Very Good/Excellent on metals, plastics, glass, rubber and wood, then per-family decision trees. 3M guide: 6 chemistries described (epoxy, acrylic, urethane, cyanoacrylate, anaerobic, reactive polyurethane hot melt (PUR)), about 13 product families, a 3-step selector chart and a substrate selector. Permabond guide: 8 chemistries (anaerobic, cyanoacrylate, structural (toughened) acrylic, two-part epoxy, single-part heat-cure epoxy, UV-curable, MS polymer/hybrid, polyurethane) with a surface-preparation × chemistry suitability table for roughly 70 substrates (metals, plastics, rubbers, glass, ceramics, wood, MDF, stone, concrete, composites, magnets) [uncertain count]. Permabond's '5 steps' article also briefly describes silicones, phenolics, polyimides, hot melts, plastisols, PVA and pressure-sensitive adhesives
coverage.organisation: By substrate, then by chemistry. Henkel design guides: an adhesive-family chapter (description, chemistry and cure mechanism, advantages and disadvantages), then one 2-page chapter per substrate (properties, trade names, typical uses, a shear-strength table for about 15 to 20 of their products against unfilled and filled grades, an 'Adhesive Performance' summary, the effect of surface treatments, compatibility notes). 3M: 'Step 1: select the most difficult substrate → Step 2: key attribute (e.g. general purpose, high temperature, low surface energy, oily metal) → Step 3: product family'. Permabond: 5 steps (certifications → technology → application requirements (substrate, gap, temperature, chemicals) → process → test) plus tables. The Henkel and Permabond grids work for beginners only once they know the plastic's proper name (e.g. polypropylene vs ABS). The 'most difficult substrate first' rule and the one-page chemistry × substrate ratings are the most beginner-usable parts
coverage.scope_match: medium: this is the authoritative source for how adhesive TYPES (chemistries) differ by material and use, which the project's adhesive family needs, and it gives real selection logic. But it's industrial, focused on selling products (tables list product numbers), and covers nothing else in the project's scope. Hobby glues are mostly missing (PVA wood glue, contact cement, solvent cement and starch paste appear only in passing)
coverage.taxonomy_used: By chemistry and cure mechanism. Henkel groups families as 'instant bonding' (cyanoacrylate, hot melt, light cure), 'flexible bonding and sealing' (elastomeric, silicone) and 'structural bonding' (two-step acrylic, two-part acrylic, epoxy, polyurethane), about 9 top-level categories in the Sourcebook. 3M splits 'structural adhesives' into rigid, flexible, toughened and heat-cured epoxy; MMA, low-odour and LSE/nylon-bonding acrylic; semi-rigid and flexible urethane; and instant adhesives (plastic-and-rubber vs surface-insensitive cyanoacrylate), ranked by load-bearing ability (pressure-sensitive tapes < hot melts < … < epoxy, the strongest). Permabond uses 8 product chemistries (AA, CA, ES, ET, MS/MT, PT, TA, UV). Substrates are grouped as metals / plastics / rubbers and elastomers / glass and ceramics / wood, with plastics further split by polymer and by surface energy (low-surface-energy polyolefins and fluoropolymers need primers or special acrylics)
coverage.example_types: cyanoacrylate (instant adhesive, superglue); rubber-toughened cyanoacrylate; surface-insensitive cyanoacrylate (for acidic surfaces like wood, paper, leather); cyanoacrylate with polyolefin primer (for polypropylene/polyethylene); UV/light-curing cyanoacrylate; two-part epoxy (rigid, flexible and toughened); one-part heat-cure epoxy; two-part structural acrylic (MMA, methyl methacrylate); two-step (no-mix, surface-activated) acrylic; low-surface-energy (LSE) bonding acrylic for PE/PP; light-curing (UV) acrylic; two-part polyurethane (urethane); reactive polyurethane hot melt (PUR); hot melt (EVA, polyamide, polyolefin types); silicone adhesive/sealant (RTV); MS polymer / silane-modified hybrid (flexible bonder-sealant); anaerobic adhesive (threadlocker, retaining compound; metal-only, cures without air); elastomeric/contact adhesive (solvent-based rubber); plus brief mentions of phenolic, polyimide, plastisol, PVA and pressure-sensitive adhesive (tapes)
coverage.making_methods: Industrial assembly and design engineering (automotive, aerospace, electronics, medical devices, appliances, signage, general metal and plastic fabrication, maintenance and repair). Not aimed at 3D printing, though the plastics data (ABS, ASA, acrylic, nylon, polycarbonate, PETG's relative PET, polypropylene) apply directly to printed parts
coverage.item_count: Henkel: 30 plastics, 8 metals/finishes and 26 rubbers/TPEs tested, with 7 to 9 adhesive families; the Plastics guide is 100 PDF pages, the Rubber guide 82 pages, the Metals guide 28 PDF pages (about 50 printed pages), the Sourcebook 216 pages. 3M: 28-page guide, 6 chemistries, about 13 product families. Permabond: 28-page guide, 8 chemistries, roughly 70 substrates in the surface-prep table [uncertain]
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Adhesive types only: cyanoacrylate, epoxy (rigid, flexible, toughened, heat-cure), structural acrylic (two-part MMA, two-step/no-mix, LSE-bonding), light/UV-cure acrylic, polyurethane (two-part and PUR hot melt), hot melt, silicone, MS polymer hybrid, anaerobic and elastomeric/contact adhesives. Materials: metals (aluminium, steel, stainless, copper, zinc/galvanised), about 30 plastics including hard-to-bond polyolefins and PTFE, rubbers and TPEs, glass, ceramics, wood, composites and concrete, with ratings and surface-prep advice for each. Uses: structural load-bearing, flexible or impact joints, sealing, gap filling, high temperature, solvent resistance. Anaerobic threadlockers and retaining compounds do touch the project's other families (thread locking against vibration loosening, retaining bearings: a kind of self-locking), but the other special behaviours (torque-limiting, one-way, indexing, over-centre, compliant, print-in-place, gear trains, powered connectors) are not covered
coverage.entry_structure: Adhesive-family entry: general description, chemistry and cure mechanism, advantages and disadvantages list, typical uses. Substrate entry (Henkel): typical property table, trade names, general description, typical applications, adhesive shear-strength table (psi/MPa; shading shows statistically significant effects of fillers or roughening), adhesive performance summary, surface treatment notes, compatibility notes (e.g. 'ABS is incompatible with anaerobic adhesives'). Selector chart (3M, Permabond): rows of substrates or attributes, columns of chemistries, cells rated Poor to Excellent or '-' for not suitable
coverage.audience_level: professional (design and manufacturing engineers); some sections (the Sourcebook comparison table, 3M's Q&A page, Permabond's viscosity-vs-everyday-liquids list) are readable by an advanced hobbyist

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: low to medium: dense tables of product codes, polymer acronyms (ASA, PBT, PEI, H-NBR) and lab data. But parts are very clear: one-page chemistry × substrate ratings (Poor to Excellent), plain advantages and disadvantages lists, joint-stress diagrams (shear vs peel vs cleavage), and Permabond's lovely viscosity scale (water 1 mPa·s, honey about 10,000, ketchup about 50,000, peanut butter about 250,000)
usefulness.has_images: yes: good-quality technical diagrams (joint types: lap, offset, butt, scarf, strap, cylindrical; stress-distribution curves; bond width vs overlap), bar charts (temperature performance, adhesive vs weld vs rivet vs nut-and-bolt shear strength and cost) and product photos
usefulness.has_animations: no (the PDFs are static; the Metals guide points to a Henkel 'Bonds vs. Bolts' video [uncertain whether still online]; 3M runs an online interactive selector that couldn't be opened from this environment [uncertain])
usefulness.gaps: (1) Brand-product answers: the tables recommend product numbers, not generic types, and each maker covers only its own chemistries. (2) Hobby adhesives are missing or barely covered: PVA wood glue, contact cement, solvent cement for PVC/acrylic/polystyrene, starch and paper glues, spray adhesive, foam-safe glues, and 3D-printing materials by name (PLA, PETG, TPU). (3) Needs the proper polymer name ('polypropylene', 'EPDM'), which beginners often don't know; there's no 'I don't know what plastic this is' route (e.g. recycling codes are shown in the Henkel guide, but there's no burn or float test). (4) Industrial surface treatments (chromic acid, sodium etch, plasma, corona) are beyond a hobbyist. (5) Some data are old (Henkel plastics prices quoted from 2004; volume 6 is 2011). (6) Health and safety for home users (fumes, skin) isn't a focus. (7) No mechanical-joint context beyond adhesive joint design
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: Partly. The PDFs have stable-ish URLs but are single large documents (link to the guide plus a page number, e.g. the Henkel Plastics guide p. 62 for polypropylene). Distributor mirrors (Ellsworth, tewipack) may move; Henkel's own DAM links (dm.henkel-dam.com) are official. Permabond web articles have stable URLs, e.g. https://permabond.com/adhesive-selection-5-steps-to-choosing-the-best-adhesive-for-your-situation/
usefulness.reusable_data: Not reusable as data: PDF tables only, all rights reserved. The ratings (e.g. cyanoacrylate: glass Poor, rubber Very Good) are facts that can be restated in our own words and cited, and the chemistry × substrate grid is small enough to rebuild by hand from several sources
usefulness.maintained: Mixed. 3M's selection guide was updated June 2024, and Permabond's guide in 2023 (edited 2024). Henkel's design guides haven't been updated since 2011 (Plastics, Rubber) and 2014 (Metals), but are still hosted on Henkel's own site and by distributors, and the Sourcebook 2017 is the latest seen [uncertain whether newer editions exist]. Several hosting domains (www.3m.com, permabond.com via WebFetch, loctite-consumer.co.uk) blocked or reset automated access from this environment, but PDFs on multimedia.3m.com, dm.henkel-dam.com and distributor sites opened
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) 'Choose for the most difficult material first' (3M Step 1): a strong top branch for the adhesive flow chart (e.g. if either part is polyethylene, polypropylene, PTFE or silicone rubber, go straight to the 'slippery plastics' branch: special primer plus superglue, or low-surface-energy acrylic). (2) The one-page chemistry × material rating table (Poor/Fair/Good/Very Good/Excellent for metals, plastics, glass, rubber, wood) as a compact comparison graphic for adhesive entries. (3) Per-chemistry trade-off rows: shear vs peel strength, flexibility, gap filling, temperature range, water/solvent resistance, cure time, one-part vs two-part. (4) Joint-design basics as a beginner panel: glue joints are strong in shear and compression and weak in peel and cleavage; making the joint wider helps more than making the overlap longer. (5) Viscosity explained with everyday liquids (water → honey → ketchup → peanut butter) to explain gap filling. (6) A 'will it stress-crack or melt this plastic?' compatibility check (Henkel stress-cracking table: cyanoacrylates and acrylics 'should be tested' on ABS, acrylic, polycarbonate, PVC, etc.). (7) 'Always test before trusting' as a final flow-chart step (Permabond step 5)
usefulness.design_rules_given: Yes, some numbers. 3M: optimum bond line (glue layer) thickness 0.005 to 0.020 in (about 0.13 to 0.5 mm); all structural adhesives give at least 1,000 psi overlap shear on aluminium; work life of 5 minutes or less for small, fast parts vs 20 minutes or more for large clamped assemblies; heat-cure epoxy at about 120 to 180 °C for 40 to 60 minutes. Permabond: cyanoacrylate gap fill up to about 0.5 mm (per grade); temperature ranges per chemistry (e.g. cyanoacrylate typical -54 to +82 °C, 1-part epoxy -40 to +150 °C). Henkel: shear strengths in psi/MPa per adhesive per plastic, stress-concentration tables vs bond-line gap and adhesive stiffness (modulus), temperature ranges per category (e.g. silicones up to about 204 °C typical)
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: No (3M offers an online filter-based product selector, not geometry)
usefulness.file_formats: PDF (plus web pages; 3M's interactive selector is a web app)
usefulness.terminology_value: high: authoritative for chemistry names and aliases (cyanoacrylate = instant adhesive; two-step/no-mix/surface-activated acrylic; MMA; PUR = reactive polyurethane hot melt; anaerobic; RTV silicone; MS polymer; low surface energy (LSE) plastics), stress terms (shear, peel, cleavage, tensile, compressive), joint types (lap, offset, butt, scarf, strap, cylindrical), and surface treatments (abrading, flame, corona, plasma, primer, etching). Good source for the 'proper engineering term in brackets'
usefulness.decision_support: Yes, several kinds. (a) Chemistry × substrate rating tables (Henkel Sourcebook p. 6; Permabond 5-steps article; Permabond surface-prep table with '-' not suitable / Poor / OK / Good / Very Good per chemistry for each of about 70 substrates). (b) 3M's 3-step selector chart (most difficult substrate → key attribute → product family) and a separate substrate selector. (c) Henkel measured shear-strength tables per plastic and rubber, with a written 'best performers' summary (e.g. polypropylene: primed cyanoacrylate or polyolefin-bonding acrylic give the strongest bonds). (d) Henkel Sourcebook decision trees per family (e.g. which cyanoacrylate or which epoxy). (e) Permabond's 5 steps: certifications → technology → substrate/gap/temperature/chemicals → process → test. (f) Stress-cracking compatibility table (Henkel)
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Each is the manufacturer's own testing and literature. Permabond's 2009 comparison table (cyanoacrylate / 2-part acrylic / surface-activated acrylic / 1-part epoxy / 2-part epoxy / UV) has the same layout, rows and ratings style as Henkel's Sourcebook table, so one may be adapted from the other or both from older Loctite literature [uncertain]. Overlaps with thisTOthat (a consumer material-pair selector with brand answers), with adhesive handbooks (e.g. Petrie's 'Handbook of Adhesives and Sealants', not checked here), with DIN 8593-8 (adhesive bonding as a joining process), and with Loctite's consumer gluing guides (loctite-consumer.co.uk 'Glues for every type of job', which are brand-led and mostly about superglue types)
